nodes.line: You have got a face like you can keep your mouth shut.

I'll be straight with you. I am sending back 20 papers a day from Robin Thomas and paying to have them collected, which is a business model somebody invented on purpose. It has been going on longer than I have admitted to anyone. You'll know it when you see it.

It has been three weeks. They will drop my Robin Thomas order if I can show $47 of turnover on the other side of the shop by grand final week. I have got no proof, which is exactly why I am asking. Half now if you want it. Most people don't.
Take a breath. Then say the whole thing.

nodes.line: No dramas. Come back when you are bored.

npcs.name: Cahil, paper runner at Robin Thomas

nodes.line: Right. Talk while I do this.

Nobody else has offered, so. I do the Robin Thomas round from ten past five and for the last fortnight somebody has been taking the papers off the front steps behind me. It might be nothing. It has not felt like nothing. Whatever it costs you, tell me and I will cover it.

The council knows and the council does not care. There is a dog on the Robin Thomas round that has had two of my bags and a chest freezer that hums in D that was not even mine. I would not ask if there was anyone else about. I would rather know than wonder.
Go on then. What did you find.

choices.text: The Robin Thomas Round — that's done.

nodes.line: Right you are. Mind the step.

npcs.name: Nell, lotto regular at Robin Thomas

nodes.line: You right there? I am mid-something but go on.

I have been putting it off since Easter. Nine of us at Robin Thomas have gone in on the same numbers since grand final week and one of us has stopped putting money in. You can tell me I am imagining it. Tell me after. That's the whole job. No catch.

Before you say anything: yes, I know. The agency at Prince Alfred Square closed six months before Robin Thomas started struggling, and I would very much like to know what they know. I would have sorted it myself a year ago. Be polite about it. It costs nothing.
You came back. That already puts you ahead.

choices.text: The Syndicate, Robin Thomas — that's done.

nodes.line: Fair enough. You know where I am.

It has been three weeks. Now that it is documented, Pymble is owed $49 in storage and the only person who can pay it is the person not answering. I have got no proof, which is exactly why I am asking. Half now if you want it. Most people don't.
Right. Tell me and do not soften it.

choices.text: The Unclaimed Falcon, Pymble — that's done.

nodes.line: Right you are. Mind the step.
Don't stand in the doorway, mate, come round.

The council knows and the council does not care. Somebody has been coming into the Pymble yard after quarter to six to use the air line, and last week they used the compressor as well. I would not ask if there was anyone else about. I would rather know than wonder.

nodes.line: Long day. Say what you came to say.

I have been putting it off since Easter. My car has been at Pymble since the first of the month and every time I ring, the quote has grown by about $17. You can tell me I am imagining it. Tell me after. That's the whole job. No catch.

Before you say anything: yes, I know. The insurance assessor who signs off every job at Pymble works out of Turramurra, and he has never once seen the car he is assessing. I would have sorted it myself a year ago. Be polite about it. It costs nothing.
Well? I can read your face from here.

I'll be straight with you. People leave things at the Denistone roller door after twenty past four and by morning it is rained on and it is our problem and our tip fee. It has been going on longer than I have admitted to anyone. You'll know it when you see it.

It has been three weeks. The photos worked, which means Denistone can claim back the $43 we have paid to throw away other people's furniture since every second Friday. I have got no proof, which is exactly why I am asking. Half now if you want it. Most people don't.
Sit. Talk. Then I will decide how I feel.
